title: Unpaid care is a gendered time-and-work infrastructure whose effects depend on formal services, household position, and digital support
source_unit: European Institute for Gender Equality, CARE Survey second-wave technical report
geography: All 27 EU Member States; population aged 16–74; fieldwork October–December 2024

care_scope.value: informal long-term care, informal childcare, housework, leisure, and volunteering

observations.method: EIGE commissioned a cross-national computer-assisted web survey using online panels, quotas for age, sex, and region, and post-fieldwork weights incorporating education, parents of children under 12, and long-term caregiver status.
observations.uncertainty: The sample is recruited from non-probability online panels; weighting improves alignment on selected characteristics but does not make the survey equivalent to a probability sample or a time-use diary.
observations.subgroup: Women and men, parents caring for children under 12, informal long-term caregivers, migrants, and households with varying employment and care arrangements.
observations.counterinterpretation: A large harmonized sample can reveal patterned differences without establishing that gender, formal-care access, employment, or household structure caused any individual outcome.

informal_formal_link.value: the survey is designed to examine interactions between informal care, access to formal care services, employment, and work–life balance

policy_target.value: childcare, long-term care, formal-care access, and the work–life effects of care responsibilities

time_conversion.value: care responsibility can be converted into constrained employment, leisure, volunteering, and schedule flexibility

observations.method: Cross-national questionnaire design linking care provision and service access with employment, work–life balance, individual activities, and household characteristics.
observations.uncertainty: The technical report documents the design and measurement route; the report alone does not provide a causal estimate of lost earnings, hours, health, or career progression.
observations.subgroup: Informal caregivers, parents of young children, employed and non-employed adults, migrants, and people with different access to formal care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Care can also produce meaning, reciprocity, skills, and social connection; treating all unpaid care as a loss would miss its relational and cultural value.

observations.period: 2024 fieldwork; care, technology, transport, and environmental routines

digital_tools.value: the second wave includes digital tools used in informal care

transport.value: the questionnaire includes transport use in relation to care activities

eco_considerations.value: the questionnaire explores eco-friendly considerations in informal care

infrastructure_route.value: care is organized through time, mobility, digital tools, household resources, and formal services rather than through a single home-based activity

observations.method: Questionnaire expansion in the second wave, with thematic modules on informal care, individual and social activities, transport, digital tools, and environmental considerations.
observations.uncertainty: Inclusion of a topic measures its visibility and reported experience; it does not establish that digital or low-carbon tools reduce care burden, improve quality, or distribute work equally.
observations.subgroup: Caregivers, care recipients, parents, migrants, people with different transport access, and households with different digital resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital tools and transport may add coordination or surveillance burdens, and greener care options may be inaccessible where time, money, or services are scarce.

longitudinal_comparison.value: the second wave builds on a first wave conducted in 2022, enabling monitoring of change over time

intersectional_analysis.value: individual and household characteristics are collected to support intersectional analysis

microdata_route.value: EIGE reports that survey microdata are to be made accessible through an open data archive in 2026

institutional_use.value: care evidence is intended to feed monitoring of the European care strategy and the Gender Equality Index

observations.method: Repeated cross-national survey design with published technical documentation, selected indicators in EIGE’s Gender Statistics Database, and a planned open-data archive for microdata.
observations.uncertainty: A repeated survey improves monitoring potential but does not guarantee identical respondents, identical country conditions, causal identification, or equal data quality across Member States.
observations.subgroup: Policy analysts, care systems, employers, households, caregivers, parents, migrants, and gender-equality institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Better measurement can support policy while still leaving unresolved questions about service quality, bargaining power, unpaid-care valuation, and whether institutions act on the evidence.

related_sources.claim: Official EIGE publication page and technical-report metadata.
Complementary ILO route on migrant labor in care work and the organization of paid and unpaid care.

boundary: This record adds a European care-and-time infrastructure route across unpaid long-term care, childcare, housework, leisure, volunteering, formal services, employment, transport, digital tools, migration, and work–life balance. It uses EIGE’s published survey design and scope, not respondent-level results, a probability sample, time-use diaries, causal estimates, observed service quality, wage histories, or proof that care responsibility produces one universal gender or labor-market outcome.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official EIGE CARE Survey second-wave technical-report PDF reviewed for survey scope, sample size, EU-27 coverage, fieldwork dates, questionnaire domains, weighting route, and planned data-access route.
